outcome: Nothing has settled the question since 26 January 2024. The one in-window event is a January 2026 computation by Max A. Alekseyev (arXiv:2601.17832, submitted 25 Jan 2026) reporting no almost perfect numbers other than the powers of 2 below 10^33, and no odd one other than 1 below 10^47; I found no independent check, journal version, or citing paper for that bound, and Wikipedia, MathWorld and the OEIS entries still describe the existence question as open.
problem_asks: (1) Existence: whether some positive integer n satisfies sigma(n) = 2n - 1 (an almost perfect number) and is not a power of 2. (2) Equivalently, whether every almost perfect number is a power of 2; the converse, that every power of 2 is almost perfect, is known. (3) The statement does not restrict parity or the shape 2^r·b² with b odd, so even and odd candidates are both in scope; the odd case (any odd almost perfect number greater than 1) is a sub-case of (1). The statement asks for existence or nonexistence of such an n, not for a bound on the smallest one, so a search finding none below some size does not by itself answer it.

events.what_happened: Kishore's result that an odd almost perfect number greater than 1 has at least six distinct prime factors (omega(n) >= 6). Wikipedia's reference list cites Kishore, 'On odd perfect, quasiperfect, and odd almost perfect numbers', Mathematics of Computation 36 (154), 1981, pp. 583-586, for this. One search snippet instead attributes the omega >= 6 result to a 1978 Kishore paper in Mathematics of Computation. The AMS record returned HTTP 403 and zbMATH returned HTTP 403, so the year is not settled; I did not read the paper itself.
events.delivers: For odd almost perfect n > 1 only: n has at least six distinct prime factors. This restricts any odd counterexample to the question; it exhibits no almost perfect number and checks no range.
events.remains: Whether any odd almost perfect number greater than 1 exists at all, and the whole even case (whether any even non-power of 2 is almost perfect).
events.direction: Constrains any odd counterexample; it neither proves nor disproves that one exists. Later sources (Wikipedia, Encyclopedia of Mathematics, and a 2019 arXiv paper on deficient-perfect numbers, arXiv:1906.09947) restate it, but I found no independent re-verification.

events.what_happened: Dagal and Dris (arXiv:1308.6767, first version 14 Aug 2013; Dagal later removed as author; Dris sole author in the version I read, v7 7 Oct 2016) give a characterisation: n is almost perfect if and only if I(n) - 1 < D(n) <= I(n), where I(n) = sigma(n)/n is the abundancy index and D(n) is the deficiency.
events.delivers: A reformulation of the condition sigma(n) = 2n - 1 in terms of the abundancy index and deficiency. It contains no bound and says nothing about powers of 2 specifically.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: the criterion does not decide whether any non-power of 2 satisfies it.
events.direction: Neither for nor against: a characterisation used as a tool by Antalan and Dris (below).
people: Keneth Adrian P. Dagal (listed on v1, removed later)

events.what_happened: Antalan and Dris, 'Some New Results On Even Almost Perfect Numbers Which Are Not Powers Of Two', arXiv:1602.04248, 7 pages, MSC 11A25. The abstract says: 'In particular, we show that 2^(r+1) < b, if 2^r b^2 is an even almost perfect number.' Theorem 2.1 in the version read (v4) states that if 2^r b^2 is almost perfect with gcd(2,b) = 1 and b > 1, then r < log2(b) - 1. Theorem 2.4 gives I(b^2) bounds and deduces 3 does not divide b when r = 1, and 7 does not divide b when r > 1. The introduction states it is currently an open problem to determine whether the only even almost perfect numbers are of the form 2^k, k >= 1.
events.revisions: v1 7 Feb 2016; v2 18 Feb 2016; v3 24 Mar 2016; v4 5 Feb 2017 (the version whose text I read). I did not confirm that v1 already carries the 2^(r+1) < b argument, so the date may move if it does not.
events.delivers: Restricted to even almost perfect numbers of the form 2^r·b² with b odd and greater than 1: a lower bound on b in terms of r (b > 2^(r+1)) and divisibility constraints (3 does not divide b when r = 1; 7 does not divide b when r > 1). It is a structural constraint on any such counterexample. It exhibits none and checks no range.
events.remains: Whether any even almost perfect number that is not a power of 2 exists (the paper leaves this open), the odd case, and the whole of the bullet's existence question.
events.direction: Constrains any counterexample of the form 2^r·b²; it neither proves nor disproves existence.
people: John Rafael M. Antalan (Central Luzon State University)
Jose Arnaldo B. Dris (Far Eastern University)

events.what_happened: Max A. Alekseyev (George Washington University), 'Computing bounded solutions to linear Diophantine equations with the sum of divisors', arXiv:2601.17832, submitted 25 Jan 2026 (single version; math.NT with cs.DM cross-list). Section 5.1 states: 'With our method, we establish that no other almost-perfect numbers exist below 10^33, which took about 6540 core-hours.' and 'For the odd almost-perfect number other than 1, we establish that none exist below 10^47, which took about 1272 core-hours.' The method is a SageMath implementation for solving a·sigma(n) = b·n + c up to a bound U, parallelised with MapReduce. The abstract frames the result as 'significantly lift[ing] the existence bounds in open questions about quasiperfect and almost-perfect numbers', and §5.1 says the existing literature 'does not seem to give an explicit lower bound on almost-perfect non-powers of 2'. The paper does not state a theorem about almost perfect numbers beyond these computed bounds.
events.revisions: v1 only (25 Jan 2026), per the arXiv abstract page as fetched on 11 Oct 2026.
events.delivers: A finite computation: no almost perfect number other than the known powers of 2 is below 10^33 (the wording says 'no other almost-perfect numbers exist below 10^33', which covers both parities), and no odd almost perfect number other than 1 is below 10^47. So any non-power-of-2 almost perfect number, if one exists, is at least 10^33, and any odd one is at least 10^47. This restricts the size of a counterexample; it gives no structural constraint, no argument valid for all n, and no counterexample.
events.remains: Whether any non-power-of-2 almost perfect number exists above 10^33 (any parity) or above 10^47 (odd), and the universal claim that every almost perfect number is a power of 2. The paper itself calls these questions open.
events.directly_checkable: The search code is public at https://github.com/maxale/multiplicative_functions. The repository page lists sigma_linear_eq.sage; the paper (§4.6) names the function res_solve_sigma_abc. I saw the file listing but did not read the file, so the function name and the 10^33 and 10^47 runs are unverified against the code.
events.doubts: Single-author SageMath computation with no independent reimplementation, rerun, or review that I could find; a single preprint version with no journal reference; no error identified in any step. The bound comes from my reading of a summarising fetch of §5.1, not verbatim text; the numbers also appear in a search snippet with the same wording.
events.direction: Every searched n below 10^33 is a power of 2 (and every odd n other than 1 below 10^47 is absent), so the computation points toward the powers-of-2 answer without deciding the question, since the question quantifies over all n.

ai.disclosed_cost: About 6540 core-hours for the all-parity search below 10^33 and about 1272 core-hours for the odd search below 10^47 (§5.1); runs used at most 80 cores (§6).

events.what_happened: Toyohara, Tao and Yao, 'Every quasiperfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors', arXiv:2608.02066, submitted 3 Aug 2026. It concerns quasiperfect numbers (sigma(n) = 2n + 1), a different problem from this bullet. It is recorded here because it is the nearest AI-credited result I found. Its acknowledgements say the mathematics 'was produced in an AI-assisted workflow' and credit 'AI systems (Anthropic's Claude, principally the Fable 5 and Opus model series ...) [which] carried out the computations, discovered and proved the lemmas, wrote and checked the Lean formalizations', while 'the human authors directed the campaign, made the methodological and editorial decisions, reviewed the results, and take responsibility for the content.' The paper does not mention almost perfect numbers or sigma(n) = 2n - 1.
events.revisions: v1 only, as far as the abstract page shows.
events.delivers: Not this problem. It establishes for quasiperfect numbers (sigma(n) = 2n + 1) that any such n has omega(n) >= 8, per its abstract. It does not touch sigma(n) = 2n - 1, so it neither restricts nor settles the almost perfect question.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks; this event has no bearing on it.

machine_checked.system: Lean: the paper's own 'qp_lean' library (19 modules, 259 theorems, 'zero sorry', no mathlib, kernel decide only), plus machine enumeration

events.doubts: The sorry-free status is the authors' own claim; I did not run the Lean code. The result is AI-credited by the authors, and I found no human public reading of it.
events.direction: Not applicable to this bullet; the claimed lower bound on omega(n) is for quasiperfect numbers.

disputes.summary: The year of Kishore's odd-almost-perfect result is given as 1981 (Math. Comp. 36, 583-586) by Wikipedia and as 1978 by a search snippet from a 2019 arXiv paper. Both are pre-window, so this affects attribution only.

summary: Across 40 searches and about 30 opened sources, the in-window picture is one computational preprint and no resolution. The Wikipedia lead (last edited 1 Nov 2025, per the fetched page) still poses the question as open and does not mention the 2026 computation; MathWorld (last updated 2 Oct 2026) and the OEIS comments on A000079 and A237588 (the latter a conjecture that a(n) = 0 iff n is a power of 2, last modified 11 Oct 2026) also still describe the question as open. The pre-window literature consists of Dris's 2013 abundancy-index criterion, Kishore's odd-case bound (ω(n) ≥ 6), and Antalan–Dris's 2016 even-case constraint (2^(r+1) < b for 2^r·b² almost perfect), which constrain a counterexample without exhibiting one. The in-window event is Alekseyev (arXiv:2601.17832, 25 Jan 2026), who reports by SageMath search that no almost perfect number other than powers of 2 lies below 10^33 and no odd one other than 1 lies below 10^47; I read the bounds from a summarising fetch of the paper's §5.1 and did not read the code. Whether this event moves the problem is a close call. Reading one: the question is existential over all n, so finite searches move nothing, as with Collatz verification. Reading two: the smallest possible non-power-of-2 almost perfect number is a quantity the question concerns, and the search raises its lower bound, as with the abc exceptional-set bound. The author's own framing ('lift the existence bounds') sides with the second reading. The AI search found no AI-credited work on this problem: AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv:2605.22763, 21 May 2026) and Epoch's OEIS Open benchmark (arXiv:2608.11941) each report settling OEIS conjectures, but A237588, the OEIS conjecture that is this problem's 'only powers of 2' claim, is absent from the 492-conjecture set in both the Epoch results repository (conjectures.json, read in full by summarising fetch) and the DeepMind formal-conjectures OEIS mapping (auto_oeis branch, summarising fetch; direct grep was refused). The one AI-credited result near this problem, arXiv:2608.02066 (Aug 2026), concerns quasiperfect numbers, not almost perfect ones, and is recorded as a discounted event.
competing_reading: Read strictly, the 10^33 and 10^47 searches contribute nothing toward the existence question, since the bullet asks whether any such number exists and a finite search, like Collatz verification to 2^71, changes no universal or existential claim. Read the other way, the bullet's quantity is the smallest non-power-of-2 almost perfect number, and the search moves its lower bound by roughly 20 orders of magnitude for the odd case; that is the abc-style reading. The paper's own framing favours the second reading, but the first is the more conventional view of finite computations on existence problems.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A peer-reviewed or independently re-run version of the 10^33 and 10^47 computations, and confirmation that res_solve_sigma_abc in the public code implements the stated search. (b) A statement from the bullet's maintainers or the literature on whether lower bounds on the smallest counterexample count as movement on this question. (c) Any later paper or OEIS comment that cites arXiv:2601.17832 for almost perfect numbers, or any proof that every almost perfect number is a power of 2, which would settle the bullet outright.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether a non-power-of-2 almost perfect number exists. Alekseyev's 2026 search below 10^33 (and odd below 10^47) is a finite check of a universal statement, so it is instances under F5; the abc-style reading in competing_reading fails because the statement asks for existence, not for the size of the smallest counterexample. The quasiperfect paper concerns sigma(n)=2n+1, a different problem, so it is a variant; its AI credit is genuine for that paper (the acknowledgements say the AI discovered and proved the lemmas) but bears on nothing here. The pre-snapshot Kishore omega>=6 and Antalan-Dris 2^(r+1)<b constraints are coded as bounds on properties of a hypothetical counterexample; the Dris criterion is a reformulation (none). Kishore is marked digested as a Mathematics of Computation paper.
judgement.doubts: Kishore and Antalan-Dris could arguably be none rather than bound (necessary conditions on a hypothetical counterexample rather than a quantity the statement names); both are pre-snapshot and neither resolves anything, so the problem's outcome is unaffected. Kishore's year (1978 vs 1981) is unsettled but pre-window either way.
